The cell you dequeued is a recycled object that still holds the last row's image, and an older async load is finishing into it — cancel that work and clear the state in `prepareForReuse`, then check identity when the load returns.

Reuse recycles the **view**, never the data. A dequeued cell arrives with every subview, layer property, gesture recognizer and observer it had at its previous index path. The collection view restores only `isSelected` and `isHighlighted` for the new index path; everything you set yourself survives.

### What prepareForReuse must undo
- Call `super.prepareForReuse()` first.
- Cancel the in-flight `Task` or `URLSessionDataTask` and drop the handle.
- Clear anything an async result writes into — `imageView.image = nil` above all.
- Tear down subscriptions, KVO observers, timers and delegate back-references the cell created.

### What it must not do
Do not reset text, colours or constraints that your configuration step always sets. That is wasted work on every dequeue, and it hides the real bug: a configure path that forgot a field and only looked right because the previous cell left the right value behind.

Cancelling is not sufficient on its own. A request that already returned can still deliver its completion after the cell moved on. Store the item identifier the load was started for and discard the result if the cell now shows something else.

Rule of thumb: `prepareForReuse` cancels and clears, `configure` sets every field unconditionally. Note that a freshly created cell never gets `prepareForReuse`, so it can never be the place where a value is first set.

An item is one cell's slot, a group arranges items along an axis, a section applies scrolling and insets to a repeating group, and the layout holds the sections — and every fractional dimension is a fraction of the item's **container**, which is its group, not the screen.

That last point is the one people get wrong. A `.fractionalWidth(1.0)` item inside a group that is itself `.fractionalWidth(0.5)` is half the collection view wide, not full width. Groups nest freely because a group *is* an item, so a hero-plus-two-thumbnails row is one horizontal group holding a big item and a vertical group.

### The three dimensions
- `.fractionalWidth(_:)` / `.fractionalHeight(_:)` — a ratio of the container's corresponding side. Cross-axis fractions are legal too: `.fractionalWidth(0.5)` as a *height* gives a 2:1 tile that stays square-ish on every screen.
- `.absolute(_:)` — points. Correct for a fixed-height row, wrong for anything holding text.
- `.estimated(_:)` — a starting guess for a self-sizing element. UIKit lays it out at that size, measures the real content, and re-runs the section. The number only needs to be in the right neighbourhood.

### The overflow trap
Two `.fractionalWidth(0.5)` items already consume the whole group, so adding `interItemSpacing` pushes the second one off the edge. Put the gutters in each item's `contentInsets` instead: insets shrink content inside a slot the layout already reserved, so the arithmetic still adds to 1.0.

Use the `sectionProvider` initialiser when the shape depends on width — the closure receives an `NSCollectionLayoutEnvironment` whose `container.effectiveContentSize` and `traitCollection` let one layout serve phone and iPad.

Give the section an `orthogonalScrollingBehavior` and do the scaling in its `visibleItemsInvalidationHandler`, which hands you every visible item plus the live offset on each frame of that scroll.

An orthogonal section is hosted inside its own private scroll view that the compositional layout creates for you. That is why the outer collection view's `contentOffset` never changes as you swipe the carousel, and why `scrollViewDidScroll` on your delegate stays silent — the handler is the only place that sees the horizontal offset.

### Choosing the behaviour
- `.continuous` — free scrolling, no snapping.
- `.continuousGroupLeadingBoundary` — free, but settles with a group's leading edge aligned.
- `.paging` — pages the width of the collection view.
- `.groupPaging` / `.groupPagingCentered` — one group per swipe, the centred variant leaving a peek of the neighbours. This is the carousel you want.

Since iOS 17 `section.orthogonalScrollingProperties` adds `decelerationRate` and `bounce` without a custom layout.

### Inside the handler
Each `NSCollectionLayoutVisibleItem` exposes `frame`, `indexPath`, `representedElementCategory` and three mutable properties — `transform`, `alpha` and `zIndex` — that apply immediately without a layout pass. Compute the distance from the item's `midX` to the offset plus half the container width, and map that to a scale.

Two traps. Calling `invalidateLayout()` in there re-enters the handler and stutters or loops forever. And the closure is retained by the layout, which the collection view retains: capture `self` weakly or capture nothing at all, and keep the body allocation-free — it runs on every scroll frame, sometimes 120 times a second.

A decoration item for the section background and an item-anchored supplementary item for the badge — the decoration never touches your data source, the badge does.

### Decoration items
`NSCollectionLayoutDecorationItem.background(elementKind:)` goes into `section.decorationItems` and draws behind that section's cells. It is created and positioned entirely by the layout: no index path from the data source, no `supplementaryViewProvider` case, nothing to keep in a snapshot. Give it `contentInsets` to pull the card in from the section's edges.

The trap is registration. Because the data source never sees it, the only place the view class is named is `layout.register(_:forDecorationViewOfKind:)`. Forget that call and the layout raises on first display, complaining it cannot load a view for the kind.

### Supplementary items
- **Boundary** — `NSCollectionLayoutBoundarySupplementaryItem(layoutSize:elementKind:alignment:)` in `section.boundarySupplementaryItems` for headers and footers, with `pinToVisibleBounds = true` for sticky ones. The same type in `UICollectionViewCompositionalLayoutConfiguration.boundarySupplementaryItems` gives a global header above every section.
- **Anchored** — `NSCollectionLayoutSupplementaryItem(layoutSize:elementKind:containerAnchor:)` passed to `NSCollectionLayoutItem(layoutSize:supplementaryItems:)`. Its `NSCollectionLayoutAnchor` takes edges plus a `fractionalOffset`, which is how a badge sits half outside its cell's corner.

Supplementaries go through `dataSource.supplementaryViewProvider`, and returning `nil` for a kind the layout asked for is a crash, not a blank space — handle every kind you declared. Use a header with `.estimated` height so it grows with Dynamic Type.

`UICollectionLayoutListConfiguration` — it turns a compositional layout, or a single section of one, into a UITableView-styled list with separators, swipe actions and accessories built in.

### Two shapes
- `UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout.list(using: config)` when the whole screen is a list.
- `NSCollectionLayoutSection.list(using:layoutEnvironment:)` inside a `sectionProvider` when one section is a list and the others are grids. This is the reason lists moved into collection views at all: you can no longer be forced to rewrite the screen because section three became a carousel.

### What the configuration carries
- `appearance`: `.plain`, `.grouped`, `.insetGrouped`, `.sidebar`, `.sidebarPlain`.
- `headerMode` / `footerMode`: `.none`, `.supplementary`, or `.firstItemInSection` for outline-style headers that are real items.
- `leadingSwipeActionsConfigurationProvider` and the trailing twin, each returning a `UISwipeActionsConfiguration`.
- `separatorConfiguration` for colour and visibility, plus `itemSeparatorHandler` for per-row overrides. Constrain your content to the cell's `separatorLayoutGuide` to make the inset line up with text.

Rows are `UICollectionViewListCell`, so `defaultContentConfiguration()` gives you the system text-and-image layout and `cell.accessories` gives you disclosure indicators, reorder grips and delete controls declaratively.

The trap is the swipe provider. It receives an `IndexPath`, which is meaningless the moment a snapshot lands, so resolve it through `dataSource.itemIdentifier(for:)` immediately. It is also stored on the layout for the screen's lifetime, so capture `self` weakly — and remember the action handler must apply the snapshot itself; the row does not delete on its own.

Because both remove a class of bug the string-and-outlet approach could not: the registration ties a cell type to an item type at compile time, and the configuration makes the cell's appearance a value you hand over rather than a set of properties you mutate.

### CellRegistration
`UICollectionView.CellRegistration<Cell, Item>` is generic over both, so the handler receives an already-typed cell and item — no identifier string to typo, no `as! MyCell` cast, no registration call to forget. `dequeueConfiguredReusableCell(using:for:item:)` registers the class on first use.

The trap: the registration must be created **once** and stored. Building one inside the cell provider closure creates a fresh registration per dequeue, so nothing is ever recycled and scrolling collapses. Make it a `let` or a `lazy var` on the controller.

The handler also runs on `reconfigureItems`, not only on dequeue, which is why it should be a pure function of the item.

### UIContentConfiguration
`cell.defaultContentConfiguration()` returns a `UIListContentConfiguration` — a value type carrying `text`, `secondaryText`, `image` and their properties, already wired to Dynamic Type and the current appearance. Because it is a value, you copy it into a `var`, mutate, and assign back; reading `cell.contentConfiguration` and mutating in place changes nothing on screen.

State becomes declarative through `UICellConfigurationState`. Override `updateConfiguration(using:)` or set `configurationUpdateHandler`, and UIKit calls it whenever selection, highlight, disabled, focus or a custom state changes. That is why you never flip a cell's colours from `didSelectItemAt` any more — you describe the cell for a state and let UIKit decide when that state applies.

The item type is an **identity**, not a value: with `Hashable` synthesized over every stored property, changing the title produces a different identifier, and the diff can only read that as one row leaving and another arriving.

Make the snapshot hold stable ids — `UUID`, a server id, a `Todo.ID` — and have the cell registration read the current values out of a store keyed by that id. Identity in the snapshot, data in the store. Then an edit keeps the same identifier and the row stays put, its selection intact and its cell instance alive.

### apply
- `apply(_:animatingDifferences:)` computes the difference against the current state and performs it. Since iOS 15 `animatingDifferences: false` still diffs, just without animation.
- When you genuinely want to throw everything away — a language switch, a fresh login — call `applySnapshotUsingReloadData(_:)`. That is the explicit replacement for the old habit of passing `false` to get a `reloadData`.
- A snapshot is a value type. `dataSource.snapshot()` hands you a copy; mutate it and apply it back. It is not a live window on the data source.

### Which queue
You may call `apply` from a background queue, but every call has to come from the **same** queue, including the very first one. Mixing a background apply with a main-thread apply is a data race that shows up as a corrupt-update crash under load, not as a warning. Pick main or pick one serial queue, and hold that choice for the screen's lifetime.

One consequence worth internalising: because the diff sees only identifiers, an unchanged identifier whose data changed produces no update at all. Making that visible has to be recorded in the snapshot explicitly.

The identifiers in one snapshot must form a set, and a struct with synthesized `Hashable` makes two rows that merely *look* alike the same identifier — that is where most duplicates come from.

### Where they come from
- Synthesized conformance over all stored properties, and two rows share every value: two "—" placeholders, two untitled drafts, two zero-amount lines.
- The same identifier appended to two sections, usually a "recent" list overlapping an "all" list.
- A server payload that genuinely repeats an id, or a paged API returning page 2 with an item from page 1.
- A class item whose `Hashable` covers mutable state. The snapshot holds the reference, you mutate the object, its hash changes underneath the diff, and the next `apply` either crashes or diffs nonsense. Use an immutable id.

The assertion fires when the snapshot is applied; newer SDKs also trap in the `appendItems` that introduces the duplicate, which is far easier to read. Write `==` and `hash(into:)` against the id alone and this class of bug disappears.

### How the diff decides
Matching is by identifier only, per section:

1. In both snapshots at a different position — a **move**.
2. Only in the new snapshot — an **insert**.
3. Only in the old one — a **delete**.
4. In both at the same position — **nothing happens**, whatever the model now contains.

Case four is the one that surprises people: the diff cannot see inside your identifier, so a changed title at an unchanged id is invisible until you record it in the snapshot yourself with `reconfigureItems` or `reloadItems`.

`snapshot.reconfigureItems([id])` — it re-runs your cell provider against the *same* live cell object, while `reloadItems` throws that cell away and dequeues a fresh one.

### What each one does to the cell
- `reloadItems` — the diff treats the item as removed and re-inserted. The old cell goes back to the reuse pool, `prepareForReuse` runs, a new cell is dequeued and configured from scratch. Everything the cell was holding is gone: the decoded image, a running animation, first-responder status, a half-typed text field, the scroll offset of a nested collection view.
- `reconfigureItems` (iOS 15 and later) — no dequeue, no `prepareForReuse`. UIKit calls your `CellRegistration` handler again with the cell that is already on screen, so it only receives new values. Selection and highlight state survive, and so does anything mid-flight.

### Where people go wrong
- If the item identifier *is* the model value — a struct whose synthesised `==` covers every field — then changing a field changes the identifier, and the diff sees a delete plus an insert no matter which method you call. Identifiers have to be stable ids; the content belongs in a lookup keyed by that id.
- `reconfigureItems` only works on an item the snapshot already contains. A brand-new row is `appendItems`, not a reconfigure.
- Outside diffable data sources the same pair exists directly on the view: `collectionView.reconfigureItems(at:)` and `reloadItems(at:)`.

Rule of thumb: reload means "this is a different thing now", reconfigure means "same thing, new values". Nearly every update driven by a live model is the second one, and across a large snapshot reconfigure is dramatically cheaper because nothing is torn down.

In the `NSDiffableDataSourceSectionSnapshot`, not in the cell and not in the flat snapshot — so a section snapshot you rebuilt from scratch is expanded exactly the way you just built it, and the refresh threw the user's choice away.

### Building the hierarchy
- A section snapshot describes one section as a tree. `append(items)` with no parent gives you roots; `append(children, to: parent)` nests them.
- `dataSource.apply(sectionSnapshot, to: .settings, animatingDifferences: true)` replaces that one section and leaves the others untouched.
- `expand(_:)`, `collapse(_:)` and `isExpanded(_:)` are the whole state API. The disclosure triangle is a cell accessory — `.outlineDisclosure(options: .init(style: .header))` — and it drives the section snapshot for you, with no gesture code.

### Carrying the state across a rebuild
- Read the current snapshot first with `dataSource.snapshot(for: section)`, record which items report `isExpanded`, rebuild, then `expand` those again.
- The flat `dataSource.snapshot()` is not a substitute: it has no parents and no expansion state, so a hierarchy round-tripped through it comes back flat.
- `sectionSnapshotHandlers.willExpandItem` and `willCollapseItem` are where you persist the choice, or lazily fetch children the first time a group opens.

The trap is keeping your own `isExpanded` flag on the model as well. Now two sources of truth disagree, and the one the collection view believes is always the section snapshot — your flag just makes the bug harder to see.

Every cell the collection view has not measured yet contributes its *estimated* height to the content size, and each time a real measurement replaces an estimate the total changes and everything below the finger shifts.

### How self-sizing actually runs
- In a compositional layout, `.estimated(n)` on the group is what opts a section into measuring; the item is usually `.fractionalHeight(1.0)` so it fills whatever the group turns out to be. `.absolute` never measures at all.
- Measurement is `systemLayoutSizeFitting` on the `contentView`, so the cell needs an unbroken constraint chain from its top edge to its bottom edge. One missing bottom constraint and the cell keeps its estimate forever.
- `preferredLayoutAttributesFitting(_:)` is the override point. The default asks Auto Layout for a size; you override it when you need to pin the width as required and leave only the height free.

### Making the jump go away
- Shrink the error. The shift is exactly the accumulated difference between your estimates and the truth, so an estimate near the real average makes it invisible.
- Cache measured heights per item id and hand back `.absolute` for the ones you already know.
- Don't discard measurements needlessly: `reconfigureItems` keeps the cell and its size, `reloadItems` re-measures from the estimate.
- On iOS 16 and later `collectionView.selfSizingInvalidation` defaults to `.enabled`, so a cell resizes itself when its configuration changes; `.enabledIncludingConstraints` also picks up Auto Layout changes made inside the cell.

The trap that reads as a layout bug: a `UILabel` with `numberOfLines = 0` and no trailing constraint measures as one enormous single line, so the cell gets a plausible height for text nobody can read.

`collectionView(_:cancelPrefetchingForItemsAt:)` — without it every fling leaves the download and decode queues stuffed with work for index paths nobody will ever look at.

### What the API does and does not promise
- Set `collectionView.prefetchDataSource` and implement `UICollectionViewDataSourcePrefetching`; `isPrefetchingEnabled` is already `true`.
- `prefetchItemsAt:` arrives ahead of display, roughly in the order the items are likely to appear. It is **not** called for the first screenful — those go straight to the cell provider — so the loading path has to exist in both places or the first screen stays blank.
- It is a hint, not a contract. UIKit can skip it entirely under load, so a cell must still cope with a cache miss.

### Making cancellation actually cancel
- Key the in-flight work by the **item identifier**, not the index path. Index paths shift the moment a snapshot is applied, and an index-path key will cancel somebody else's download.
- Cancel the `Task`, not just your bookkeeping. `URLSession`'s async methods throw at the next suspension point, but a decode or resize loop has to check `Task.isCancelled` itself.
- Cancel in `prepareForReuse` too — that covers the cell whose own request is still running when it scrolls away.

The rule that keeps it honest: prefetching is optional, cancellation is not. A prefetcher with no cancel path turns a fast scroll into a denial of service on your own network queue, and the images that eventually arrive belong to rows the user passed seconds ago.

The collection view moved the cell and the data source moved the item inside its own snapshot, but nothing wrote the new order back to the model, so the next snapshot built from that model undoes the drag.

### Reordering with a diffable data source
- `dataSource.reorderingHandlers.canReorderItem` has to return `true` for an item before UIKit will let it move at all, and a list cell needs the `.reorder()` accessory (or a drag delegate) before there is anything to grab.
- `reorderingHandlers.didReorder` hands you an `NSDiffableDataSourceTransaction` carrying `initialSnapshot`, `finalSnapshot` and a `difference` you replay onto your array with `Array.applying(_:)`. Write the model there, in that callback, before anything else can rebuild.
- For a single-section model, `transaction.sectionTransactions.first?.difference` is the per-section form of the same diff.

### While a drag is in flight
- Don't `apply` a snapshot from a socket or a timer mid-drag: the data source is already mutating and the dragged cell snaps back. Guard on `collectionView.hasActiveDrag`, stash the update, and replay it from `dragSessionDidEnd`.
- Full drag and drop — across sections, or across apps — is a different pair of protocols. `UICollectionViewDragDelegate` returns `UIDragItem`s wrapping an `NSItemProvider`; `UICollectionViewDropDelegate` answers `dropSessionDidUpdate` with a `UICollectionViewDropProposal` and does the work in `performDropWith:` using `coordinator.destinationIndexPath`.

The mental model: the transaction is the only account of what happened that the view and the model can both agree on. An index path you captured before the drag, or an offset you cached, is stale by the time the drop lands.

`layoutAttributesForElements(in:)` — it is called several times per frame, so a version that walks every item in the collection makes scrolling O(items) on every pass.

### The four pieces, and where the work belongs
1. `prepare()` — compute every attribute once and cache it. UIKit calls this after an invalidation, not per frame, and it is the only place computation belongs.
2. `collectionViewContentSize` — return the cached total. A wrong value breaks the scroll indicator and the rubber-banding before it breaks anything visible.
3. `layoutAttributesForElements(in:)` — a *lookup*. Keep the cache sorted by `minY` and binary-search the first candidate, or bucket attributes by row.
4. `layoutAttributesForItem(at:)`, plus the supplementary and decoration variants — one dictionary hit each.

### Invalidation is the other half
- `shouldInvalidateLayout(forBoundsChange:)` returning `true` unconditionally re-runs `prepare()` on every scroll frame. Return `true` only when the width actually changed.
- Return a narrow `UICollectionViewLayoutInvalidationContext` from `invalidationContext(forBoundsChange:)` and call `invalidateItems(at:)` on it, so `prepare()` can rebuild part of the cache instead of all of it.
- For self-sizing cells, `shouldInvalidateLayout(forPreferredLayoutAttributes:withOriginalAttributes:)` decides whether one measured cell forces a re-layout — compare the sizes and return `false` when nothing moved, or a single label rebuilds the world.

The trap that produces invisible headers: `layoutAttributesForElements(in:)` must return supplementary and decoration attributes too, not only cells. Anything you leave out of that array simply never appears, and nothing warns you.

In hashing and comparing your item identifiers and then animating the changes it found — and `apply` runs that diff on whatever queue you call it from, which is almost always the main one.

### Where the cost actually is
- The diff is proportional to the item count, but the cost per item is your `Hashable` conformance. An identifier that is a struct with a synthesised `==` over twenty fields hashes twenty fields ten thousand times. Make the identifier a `UUID` or a `String` and keep the content in a dictionary keyed by it.
- The animation is proportional to the number of *changes*, not the number of items. A thousand animated moves costs far more than the diff that found them. `animatingDifferences: false` skips the animation but still diffs.
- For a wholesale replacement — first load, a new search term — `applySnapshotUsingReloadData(_:)` skips the diff entirely, at the price of no animation and a lost scroll position.

### Getting it off the critical path
- You may call `apply` from a background queue, provided you do it from the **same** queue every single time and never mix in a main-queue call. Build the snapshot there too, from an immutable copy of the model.
- Coalesce. A socket emitting ten messages a second should fill a buffer that applies once every hundred milliseconds, not ten snapshots that each diff ten thousand rows.
- The async `await dataSource.apply(...)` overload is main-actor isolated; it is good for sequencing an update against an animation, not for moving work off main.

The failure that follows teams around is a duplicate-identifier crash that only appears under load: two producers built snapshots concurrently from a model that was mutating underneath them. One queue owns the model, the snapshot and the apply, or that crash is only a matter of time.

Extract the row model first — whatever `cellForRowAt` switches on becomes the item identifier of a snapshot — and pin it down with a test over that pure state-to-items function before a single UIKit type changes.

### The order that keeps the diff reviewable
1. **Row model.** Turn the implicit rows into an enum or an id type and write `func items(for state: State) -> [Row]`. Unit-test it. This is the only step that touches logic, and it carries all the risk.
2. **Container swap.** `UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout.list(using:)` with a `UICollectionLayoutListConfiguration`, plus a `UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource` over that row type. `UIListContentConfiguration` replaces `textLabel` and `detailTextLabel`, deprecated since iOS 14.
3. **Delegate methods, by kind.** Heights vanish into the layout. `didSelectRowAt` becomes `didSelectItemAt`. Swipe actions become `leading`/`trailingSwipeActionsConfigurationProvider` on the list configuration. Section titles become `headerMode = .supplementary` or `.firstItemInSection`. `willDisplay` and `didEndDisplaying` keep their names.
4. **Delete `reloadData`.** Last, once nothing else calls it.

### Proving it
- The snapshot-builder test from step 1 is the regression net worth keeping: assert the exact item order for a handful of states.
- Screenshot-diff the screen at the default text size, at the largest accessibility size, and in a right-to-left pseudolanguage — a list configuration does not lay out pixel-identically to a hand-built cell.
- UI tests for the interactions that lost their delegate method: select, swipe, reorder.
- Keep the old screen behind a flag for one release and compare the same analytics events from both.

The trap is index paths: half of a long delegate stashes one somewhere, and after a diff they are stale. Each becomes `dataSource.itemIdentifier(for:)` on the way in and `indexPath(for:)` on the way out. The second trap is redesigning in the same pull request — then no screenshot diff means anything.
